articles.title: Former White House ethics attorney: Taxpayer-funded ads could be ‘impeachable offense’
articles.summary: Former White House ethics attorney Richard Painter said the White House using taxpayer dollars for TV ads promoting President Trump could be “an impeachable...
articles.body:
Former White House ethics attorney Richard Painter said the White House using taxpayer dollars for TV ads promoting President Trump could be "an impeachable offense."

"As I told @baylisswagner of the @nytimes here, this could be an impeachable offense. @POTUS has no right to use taxpayer money for campaign ads," Painter wrote Sunday on the social platform X, referencing similar remarks he made to The New York Times .

"Congress has expressly prohibited government sponsored political propaganda, which is dangerous for democracy," added Painter, who was former President George W. Bush's chief ethics lawyer during his second term.

Multiple networks in recent days have aired the ads promoting Trump, with roughly five weeks remaining before the midterms . Republicans are fighting to maintain control of Congress next year.

One ad features audio of the president saying, "Together, we will defeat communism, socialism and Marxism in America," as singer JMSN's "Love Me" plays in the background.

The ad concludes with audio of UFC CEO Dana White calling Trump the "toughest, most resilient person that I've ever met."

Another clip features the president saying during his 2024 presidential campaign that he and his supporters "will demolish the deep state" and "expel the warmongers from our government." The war in Iran , which the U.S. and Israel launched in late February, hit the seven-month mark on Monday.

"We will rout the fake news media, and we will liberate America from these villains once and for all," the president says in the ad.

Both of the spots include disclaimers that say "Paid for by the U.S. Government." Under the Federal Election Campaign Act of 1971 , public officials cannot use taxpayer dollars for campaigning purposes.

Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have criticized the latest advertisements. Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy (Conn.) wrote on X last week , "Every taxpayer, no matter your party, should be outraged by this."

GOP Sen. John Kennedy (La.) also said Sunday the use of taxpayer money to fund ads promoting the president was "probably" illegal.

"I don't think any public official, including President Trump … or John Kennedy, should spend public money … on private ads for themselves," Kennedy told host Margaret Brennan on CBS's " Face the Nation ."

But the White House has defended the clips, claiming in a Friday release that the commercials "are clearly not campaign ads" since Trump is not on the ballot in November. The president, however, has instructed voters to "pretend" as if he is on the ballot in the midterms.

The Trump administration also highlighted past examples of the federal government airing public service announcements, such as when the George W. Bush and Obama administrations aired spots explaining new Medicare legislation and open enrollment in the Affordable Care Act marketplace, respectively.

"When prior Administrations utilized the airwaves, it was called 'public education,'" the White House release reads. "When this Administration promotes pride in our country, many of those same voices call it 'propaganda.'"

"Patriotism isn't partisan. These public service announcements are unapologetically American, clearly disclosed, and aimed at the country — not a line on the ballot," it continued.

articles.title: Far-left legal 'cartel' in the hot seat as Trump admin decides its law school gatekeeper status
articles.summary: The Trump Education Department now has 90 days to decide whether to strip the American Bar Association of its decades-long law school accreditation monopoly.
articles.body: The future of the nation's primary law school accreditor now rests in the hands of the Trump Education Department after a federal panel deadlocked 8-8 on whether to strip the American Bar Association (ABA) of its gatekeeper status following dozens of federal compliance failures. The deadlock hands the decision to Under Secretary of Education Nicholas Kent, who has up to 90 days to decide whether to revoke the ABA’s decades-long accreditation monopoly over roughly 200 law schools nationwide. In a statement to Fox News Digital, a Department of Education spokesperson confirmed that staff had already recommended stripping the ABA's gatekeeper status after finding the group out of compliance with "more than 26 recognition criteria." The advisory body—known formally as the National Advisory Committee on Institutional Quality and Integrity (NACIQI)—advises the Education Department on whether higher education accreditors meet federal standards. NACIQI Chairman Jay Greene told Fox News Digital that while the panel split 8-8 on what action to take, committee members across the board shared a core concern over how the ABA is structured. "The primary issue that troubled all members of NACIQI is that the ABA accrediting body is clearly not separate and independent from the ABA as a whole," Greene said, noting that federal law requires institutional accreditors to operate independently of trade associations. "Everyone on the committee agreed that this was a problem that required changes. The main divide was over whether the ABA was willing and able to take those steps to remedy the problem or not." WATCH: BRANDON GILL CORNERS LAW SCHOOL GATEKEEPER WITH DEI QUESTION SHE WON'T ANSWER Responding to panel criticisms of chronic noncompliance, Melissa Hart, chair of the ABA Accreditation Council, defended the organization's historic track record. "The Council has been continuously recognized by the Department of Education since 1952, being found in compliance during every regular recognition cycle for the past 74 years," Hart said in a statement. "We take accreditation and our recognition as an accreditor very seriously, and we continue to be a reliable authority for accrediting J.D. programs." However, legal advocacy groups argue the ABA's structural defects and recent policy shifts render it unfit to serve as an industry gatekeeper. Reed Rubinstein, Senior Vice President of America First Legal and former General Counsel at the Department of Education, told Fox News Digital that the ABA has "disqualified itself and undermined public faith and trust in the legal profession." EXPLOSIVE REPORT EXPOSES ‘DANGEROUS IMBALANCE’ IN LAW SCHOOL PIPELINE SHAPING HOW ELECTION CASES ARE DECIDED Rubinstein also dismissed the ABA's recent move to repeal its controversial diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) accreditation standard as a "ruse to retain power," arguing it does not cure the underlying legal flaws. "The DEI accreditation standard, from the moment it was adopted, conflicted with controlling Supreme Court rulings and the plain text of the Civil Rights Act," Rubinstein said, urging the Trump administration to permanently strip the ABA of its federal status. "The ABA's leadership has made it clear, publicly and otherwise, that it will return to its unlawful ideological agenda at its first opportunity." For more than 70 years, the ABA has operated as the sole federally recognized accreditor for U.S. law schools, granting the organization a near-monopoly over the legal profession. In almost every state, students must graduate from an ABA-accredited law school to be eligible to sit for the bar exam. Furthermore, the federal government uses the ABA's accreditation as the gatekeeper for Title IV federal student aid, meaning law schools must secure the group's stamp of approval for their students to receive federal loans. BEAUTY SCHOOL MOMS CAUGHT IN ACCREDITATION CROSSFIRE AS TRUMP ADMINISTRATION WEIGHS CONSEQUENTIAL DECISION If Under Secretary Kent ultimately moves to strip the ABA of its recognition, the decision would effectively break that national monopoly. While law schools affiliated with larger universities could rely on their broader institutional accreditors to maintain access to federal financial aid, roughly a dozen stand-alone law schools would be forced to scramble for alternative accreditation. State supreme courts would also face immediate pressure to rewrite their bar admission rules to allow graduates from non-ABA schools to take the exam. Some states have already begun taking matters into their own hands to bypass the ABA's grip. Because the legal profession is regulated directly by the judicial branch, state supreme courts hold the ultimate authority to set educational requirements for bar admission. TRUMP ADMIN URGES RETURNING EDUCATION TO STATES, CITING $3 TRILLION OF TAXES SPENT AND POOR PROFICIENCY SCORES In January, Texas became the first state in the nation to eliminate its reliance on the ABA for law school accreditation, with the Texas Supreme Court finalizing a rule to take over the approval process itself. Just nine days later, the Florida Supreme Court followed suit. By cutting ties with the organization, the Texas high court announced it would judge law schools on "simple, objective, and ideologically neutral criteria" rather than the ABA's mandates deemed by many as politically-driven. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Other states are now catching on to the rebellion against the ABA. The Ohio Supreme Court formally proposed amendments in May to establish a state-run accreditation process, while supreme courts in Tennessee, Alabama, and Washington have all recently taken steps to bypass the organization's monopoly. "The ABA’s cartel-like control over law school accreditation drives up costs, limits access, and pushes ridiculous ideological mandates over merit," Trump's DOJ said earlier this year. "Ending the Tennessee Supreme Court’s exclusive reliance will expand opportunity AND lower costs." Rubinstein noted that transferring authority back to the states marks a long-overdue correction for legal education. "State supreme courts are ultimately responsible for certifying and disciplining attorneys—there is arguably no need for a middleman," Rubinstein told Fox News Digital. "By returning actual authority over legal education directly to the courts themselves... the result should be a better-quality education for attorneys and more accountability and transparency for the public."

articles.title: Walz's 'exit interview' reflecting on his tenure sparks lawmaker debate about his legacy: 'Never serious'
articles.summary: Minnesota Democratic Gov. Tim Walz says fraud shouldn't define his legacy, but Republican lawmakers fire back with a list of grievances beyond the scandal.
articles.body: Minnesota Democratic Gov. Tim Walz reflected on his legacy in a recent interview and his comments sparked immediate pushback both online and from Republican lawmakers in the state who spoke to Fox News Digital. "Fraud — should have stopped it sooner," Walz told the Minnesota Star-Tribune in a discussion that is being dubbed an "exit interview" with the headline "Walz accepts blame for fraud but says it shouldn’t define his legacy" as he prepares to leave office in January. "We didn’t stop them. I accept that. I think there does need to be accountability with that. And part of it is that, yep, that’s with me, I’ll step aside." Walz claimed the state "immediately" took action on the fraud and then went on to suggest the true cost of the fraud, estimated at $9 billion by federal prosecutors, has been overstated and claimed President Donald Trump’s White House ballroom, expected to cost taxpayers around $300 million, was more expensive than the Minnesota fraud. WALZ APPROVAL RATING CRATERS TO LOWEST LEVEL EVER AND TRAILS TRUMP AMID MASSIVE FRAUD SCANDAL: 'TIRED OF IT' "I should have been down on those agencies a little more, but I will tell you this, in the scheme of things, all the fraud that's been prosecuted, by the way, and all the fraud that's probably out there is less than the ballroom at the White House," Walz said. "So it puts it into perspective. It doesn't make it right. Doesn't make it right." The outgoing governor then explained his hope that people will remember his other accomplishments when talking about his legacy. "Those are legacy things to address climate. They’re legacy things to address livability," Walz said. "And I get it, that fraud tainted a lot of that. It doesn’t change the fundamentals underneath it. This is the best state in the country to raise a child, and it will continue to be so because of those investments." Three Republican lawmakers in Minnesota who spoke to Fox News Digital had a different take. "Governor Walz is correct, he shouldn’t only be remembered for fraud," Minnesota state Sen. Julia Coleman told Fox News Digital. "We should remember him spending our $18 billion surplus, raising taxes $10 billion, creating an unsustainable budget, letting rioters burn down Minneapolis, hurting our students and businesses with lockdowns and pardoning a child rapist." 'WE HAVE NOT SLOWED DOWN': MINNESOTA NOT OUT OF THE WOODS ON MASSIVE FRAUD SCANDAL, EXPERT WARNS Walz has faced fierce criticism for helping approve a full pardon for Tue Lue Vang, a Laotian national convicted of repeatedly raping a girl beginning when she was 10. Critics argued the decision prioritized Vang’s immigration concerns and family ties over the severity of his crimes, with a DHS official calling it "disgusting." Minnesota Republican House Speaker Lisa Demuth is running to replace Walz in November as she heads into a matchup with Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar to be the state’s next top executive. Demuth told Fox News Digital Walz’s legacy won’t be able to overcome the fraud scandal and pointed to Klobuchar’s tight association with him. "Tim Walz's legacy will always be defined by the out-of-control fraud crisis that occurred on his watch," Demuth said. "Yet Amy Klobuchar praised him as ‘an incredible leader who delivers for the people of Minnesota.’ As the senior member of our state’s congressional delegation, Sen. Klobuchar likewise failed to address the fraud crisis and even skipped hearings on the matter in D.C. Minnesotans deserve better than four more years of Walz-style failure." Republican State Rep. Kristin Robbins chaired the last legislative session’s Fraud Prevention and State Agency Oversight Policy Committee, and she told Fox News Digital that "no matter how hard he tries to spin it, Tim Walz’s legacy will be that he allowed rampant fraud." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "He says he ‘should have stopped it sooner,’ which is obvious, but he could still be doing more NOW," Robbins said. "He has been silent on fraud for months instead of taking the actions that are STILL under his control." Robbins said Walz could have taken several steps to combat fraud, including firing senior DHS official Shireen Gandhi to send a message that abuse would not be tolerated, blocking Minnesota from seeking a SNAP waiver that allows applicants to attest to eligibility by phone without recording the call, and asking Attorney General Keith Ellison to prosecute Partners in Nutrition, a nonprofit that administered federally funded meal programs, rather than approve a settlement. "His legacy will be fraud because he continues to enable fraud, despite two years of hearings, investigative journalists, and Office of the Legislative Auditor (OLA) reports," Robbins said. "He was never serious about stopping it and still isn’t." Walz's comments not only drew scrutiny from Republican lawmakers but also sparked backlash on social media. "Walz accepts blame for fraud, but believes his loss of $9 billion in taxpayer dollars 'shouldn't define his legacy,'" the X account for Minnesota House Republicans posted on X. "It does, and Minnesotans are paying attention to his blatant disregard of their hard-earned tax dollars." Fox News Digital reached out to Walz's office for comment.

articles.title: AOC gives major hint about 2028 as Democrat civil war looms
articles.summary: Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez says she's weighing a 2028 presidential run or a challenge to Chuck Schumer's New York Senate seat after midterm elections.
articles.body: Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez's political future has remained a topic of discussion within the left wing — and there's increasing speculation that she could be set for a collision course with Democrats' top leader in Congress. The progressive rock star says she's weighing what to do next, whether it be a 2028 presidential run or a bid for the seat currently held by Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, a fellow Democrat and New Yorker. "I know there is a lot of speculation about what I will decide to do in 2028. I get asked about it nearly every interview and event," Ocasio-Cortez wrote in a recent fundraising email to supporters. The 36-year-old lawmaker with a massive social media footprint said in a recent New York Times interview that her decision, which could happen sometime after this year's midterm elections, would come down to answering the question, "Where can I do the most good?" OCASIO-CORTEZ OPENS UP ABOUT 2028 If she decides on a statewide rather than a national run, it could set up a titanic Democratic Party and generational battle between her and the soon-to-be 76-year-old Schumer, who was first elected to Congress nearly half a century ago and has served in the Senate since 1999. Ocasio-Cortez, in her interview, made clear that her decision about 2028 would not be dictated by someone else. "I don’t think that my decisions would come down to deference," she said. Meanwhile, a campaign swing the past few days throughout upstate New York by Ocasio-Cortez raised some eyebrows. While the trip was aimed at boosting fellow Democrats on the ballot in this year's elections, it sparked speculation that it was also a move by Ocasio-Cortez to build relationships far from her base in New York City. Schumer has left his 2028 plans open and has not announced whether he’ll run for yet another term. When asked about re-election, he's repeatedly said his "first focus is winning in 2026, getting back the Senate in 2026." Fox News Digital reached out to Schumer's office regarding his thinking on a potential 2028 re-election run, but didn't receive a response by the time this story was published. articles.title: How to win the vote of generation vape
articles.summary: The governing lesson is familiar: Condemnation is not a substitute for sensible policy.
articles.body:
Nearly one in five young adults now vape. Gallup’s August survey found that 9 percent of adults overall use vapes. Nicotine pouches also skew young.

We increasingly have a generation whose habits look very different from those of their parents. This is a reality progressives must acknowledge, and a voting base we should strive to serve. I learned the importance of confronting reality as mayor of Ithaca during the opioid crisis.

In 2014, three people died of heroin overdoses in Ithaca in just 10 days . We watched people die while America argued about whether harm reduction somehow condoned drug use. So, we developed the Ithaca Plan , bringing prevention, treatment, law enforcement and harm reduction together. We even proposed exploring supervised injection.

My argument then was simple: If your goal is treatment and recovery, then use evidence-based approaches to protecting people, and start by keeping them alive. Tobacco presents different risks. But the governing lesson is familiar: Condemnation is not a substitute for sensible policy. Moral judgment is not a substitute for evidence.

And the evidence has changed. The Food and Drug Administration says explicitly that no tobacco product is safe. But it also says tobacco products exist on a continuum of risk : cigarettes are the most harmful, while non-combusted products including e-cigarettes and nicotine pouches generally carry lower health risks.

In June, FDA went further, authorizing 20 Zyn nicotine pouches to carry a modified-risk claim explaining that using them instead of cigarettes lowers the risk of several major smoking-related diseases.

The evidence on vaping is strengthening too. In a July JAMA commentary , University of Massachusetts assistant professor Jamie Hartmann-Boyce addressed what she called the genuine dilemma facing doctors counseling smokers. The underlying evidence, she wrote, shows nicotine e-cigarettes are more effective for smoking cessation than FDA-approved nicotine-replacement therapies. A companion JAMA paper recommended integrating e-cigarettes into clinicians’ conversations with adults trying to quit cigarettes.

That does not make vaping harmless. Nicotine is addictive. Kids should not use it. Long-term effects require continued study. But “not harmless” and “as harmful as cigarettes” are very different statements.

For policymakers, that creates questions about what sensible regulation looks like: age verification, manufacturing standards, ingredient disclosure, restrictions on marketing to children and an FDA authorization system capable of distinguishing regulated products from illicit ones.

There is also a generational political reality worth understanding. Vaping is most prevalent among Americans under 30, and Pew currently finds registered voters in that age group prefer Democratic congressional candidates by a margin of 47 percent to 24 percent.

Those statistics overlap; they do not prove that tobacco policy determines anyone’s vote. What they do show is that millions of young Americans who are aligned with Democratic values use these products.

My experience in Ithaca taught me that shame does not make addiction disappear. Neither does pretending that people will stop doing something simply because the government wishes they would. Good public policy begins with the world as it actually exists — and reaching out a supportive hand instead of a wagging finger.

Democrats have a chance to run on these issues and be viewed as a caring but nonjudgmental party; more like cool parents and less like the worst members of a homeowners’ association board.

Svante Myrick is president of People For the American Way.

S&P Global reported that federal data showed prices for iron and steel rose 10.4% between April 2025 and April 2026, while the steel mill products index climbed 13.3%, even as domestic steel production increased. Unlike many newer U.S. steel facilities, which are smaller electric arc furnace plants, the Iowa project will be a large-scale integrated steel facility. The White House says it will be the first new "mega-steel" plant built in the United States since the 1960s. The first phase of the steel plant and the Minnesota mine together represent nearly $18 billion in investment, according to the administration. The White House estimates the first phase will generate approximately $95 billion in economic activity during construction and the plant's first decade of operation. articles.body:
Former Rep. Barbara Comstock (R-Va.) said Sunday that during this summer, President Trump “did everything he could to help Republicans lose” the upcoming midterms.

“Well, I think elections are won in the summer, and we’re now here in late September. And Donald Trump did everything he could to help Republicans lose over the summer,” Comstock said on MS NOW’s “The Weekend.”

“You know, starting with the [Iran] war, continuing all through the summer, which led the gas prices to be, you know, $4.49, and the war is not popular at all, and, of course, you know, now we have 7 percent interest rates,” she added.

As the midterms near, the president and his party are in a bit of an electoral pickle. Trump’s approval rating has slumped, the unpopular war in Iran hit the seven-month mark Monday, Democrats have outperformed Republicans in recent polling and there are widespread concerns about the economy as Election Day nears.

According to a polling average from Decision Desk HQ, Trump’s approval rating was sitting at 39.4 percent Monday morning, while his disapproval rating was 59.1 percent.

Comstock also referenced the Iran war’s effect on energy costs, with the Strait of Hormuz, a key waterway for the oil industry, closed amid the fighting. According to AAA, the average price of a gallon of regular gas in the U.S. Monday morning was about $4.48 , up from around $3.13 last year.

And last week , the average 30-year mortgage rate surpassed 7 percent, marking the first time it has done so since January 2025.

Multiple Republicans in the heartland have broken with the president on unpopular policies, with Republicans anxious about dealing with backlash from them in the midterms.

Lawmakers and candidates in Iowa, Michigan and Ohio have pushed for a rapid end to the war in Iran amid high gas and diesel costs as well as the increasing unpopularity of the conflict.

Reached for comment, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a statement that “no one can dispute the fact that President Trump has created one of the most robust coalitions in political history with the MAGA movement, and the President understands how to communicate with them.”

articles.title: States should not blindly Alabama’s use of execution by nitrogen
articles.summary: History suggests that once one state adopts a new execution method, other states are certain to follow. That explains why Louisiana wants to imitate Alabama’s embrace of nitrogen hypoxia — even though the latter has yet to get it right.
articles.body:
In a federal system like our own, states wanting to do something new often look to the experience of other states and imitate them. The results of such imitation are by no means certain.

“Sometimes,” political scientist David Schultz argues , “those policies are good ones, but more often borrowing from other states is a short-cut mechanism that results in policies that fail to deliver. States,” he adds, “become creatures of me-tooism, repeating and replicating policy initiatives found elsewhere without asking if in fact they work.”

That is as true when it comes to the death penalty as it is in any other policy area. History suggests that once one state adopts a new execution method, other states are certain to follow. That explains why Louisiana wants to imitate Alabama’s embrace of nitrogen hypoxia — even though the latter has yet to get it right.

Courts should not allow it to do so until it can show that it can get it right.

This is not the first time that we’ve seen this pattern of imitation in execution technologies. Take the electric chair, for example.

In 1888, New York adopted the chair as its execution method . As Professor Jürgen Martschukat says, “death by electrocution was widely perceived as an advance of civilization. It was part of the remodeled, modern world … and, as such, it was understood to give society a sense of elevation.”

Two years later, when New York became the first state to use that execution method, things did not go as planned, and William Kemmler died a gruesome death .

But that did not stop other states from embracing the electric chair. Between 1897 and 1908, Ohio, Massachusetts, New Jersey and Virginia chose it to replace hanging . It didn’t take long for electrocution to become the most frequently used execution method in the U.S.

Decades later, a similar pattern marked the emergence and spread of lethal injection. Oklahoma led the way , passing a law in 1977 to authorize lethal injection executions. Five years later, Texas became the first state to use the method when it executed Charles Brooks, Jr. Soon, other states followed suit.

Today, we are seeing the same pattern with America’s newest execution method, nitrogen hypoxia. It was first adopted in Oklahoma in 2015 and is now also legal in Alabama, Arkansas, Louisiana and Mississippi.

It wasn’t until January 2024 that Alabama carried out the nation’s first nitrogen hypoxia execution, putting Kenneth Smith to death. But, as the AP reports , as the gas started to flow, Smith “shook in thrashing spasms and seizure-like movements for several minutes at the start of the execution. The force of his movements caused the gurney to visibly move at least once.”

Three months later, Louisiana added nitrogen hypoxia to its menu of execution methods . And as a lawsuit filed on Sept. 4 alleges, Louisiana fully adopted Alabama’s nitrogen hypoxia procedure.

Louisiana plans to use that procedure to execute Todd Wessinger for the 1995 killings of two people at Calendar’s Restaurant in Baton Rouge. Wessinger alleges that “execution by nitrogen hypoxia creates a substantial risk of serious harm and severe pain.”

“Nitrogen hypoxia,” the suit continues, “kills by depriving a conscious person of oxygen. As oxygen deprivation intensifies, the condemned prisoner experiences severe air hunger — the primal, physical, and intensely distressing sensation of suffocation — before losing consciousness.”

The suit points out that after Louisiana authorized nitrogen hypoxia as a method of execution, corrections officials “sought to replicate Alabama’s system as closely as possible.” In fact, they considered only Alabama’s nitrogen-hypoxia protocol.

Meantime, Wessinger’s suit details the serious problems and abundant cruelty that have plagued every one of Alabama’s seven nitrogen hypoxia executions. And Wessinger reminds the court that the Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals held in June that Alabama’s nitrogen-hypoxia protocol presented “a substantial risk of serious harm that was ‘not conjectural, speculative, or doubtful.’”

All of this should be enough for the Federal District Court for the Middle District of Louisiana to stop that state from blindly imitating Alabama.

What is unfolding is an example of what Schultz calls an unverified belief that states are “laboratories of public-policy innovation.” However, “often they are no more than factories of replication, captured by political myths and doomed to re-enact failed policies.”

Todd Wessinger deserves better than to be a victim of one such failed policy.

Austin Sarat is the William Nelson Cromwell Professor of Jurisprudence and Political Science at Amherst College.

articles.title: Networks to resume TV pool coverage of Trump despite White House block of CNN
articles.summary: Major television networks plan to continue to provide pool coverage of President Trump’s daily activities this week despite the White House’s ongoing efforts to block CNN from covering the president. Each of the TV networks in the pool, including NBC, ABC, CBS and Fox, plan to fulfill their pool duties on the days they are…
articles.body:
Major television networks plan to continue to provide pool coverage of President Trump’s daily activities this week despite the White House’s ongoing efforts to block CNN from covering the president.

Each of the TV networks in the pool, including NBC, ABC, CBS and Fox, plan to fulfill their pool duties on the days they are assigned this week, The Hill confirmed on Monday, even as CNN’s ability to serve as the designated TV pool crew remained in doubt.

The major networks for several days last week pulled out of pool coverage in solidarity with CNN after Trump banned the cable channel and two other outlets from the White House over what he said was its publishing of “fake news,” which he argued put national security at risk.

The three outlets, CNN, Politico and MS NOW, sued over the ban and won last week, with a federal judge ruling the White House violated the media companies’ due process rights. Attorneys for the media companies said the ban also ran afoul of First Amendment protections.

Pool coverage of the president resumed last week after CNN and the two other outlets were let back onto the White House grounds, but tensions flared again over the weekend when CNN was blocked from covering Trump on Air Force One ahead of his trip to Tennessee.

The TV networks, which initially blasted Trump over the ban, are assessing the TV pool situation on a day-by-day basis, a person familiar with the discussions said.

A White House schedule for TV pool rotation announced Sunday listed CNN as the primary pool provider for Thursday, when Trump is slated to travel to Texas and Oklahoma for rallies.

articles.title: Talarico vs. Paxton Texas Senate race tightens as new poll drops
articles.summary: A new BIG DATA POLL offers a fresh look at the closely watched Texas Senate race between James Talarico and Ken Paxton. Here’s what the survey found.
articles.body:
A new poll finds that Democrat James Talarico is holding a slight lead over Republican Ken Paxton in the race for U.S. Senate in Texas.

A BIG DATA POLL conducted Sept. 24–26 found Talarico ahead of Paxton among registered Texas voters, 43.6% to 39.3%. Among voters likely to cast a ballot, Talarico led 44.6% to 41.6%.

When pollsters asked undecided voters which candidate they were leaning toward, the race tightened.

Talarico led Paxton 46.4% to 43.8% among registered voters and 46.8% to 44.9% among likely voters, suggesting undecided voters leaned more toward Paxton, narrowing Talarico's lead.

The poll surveyed 793 registered voters and 698 likely voters in Texas. For both groups, the margin of error is plus or minus 4 percentage points.

Here's what September polls have shown so far:

Texas Southern University (Sept. 22) — Talarico 47%, Paxton 46%.

ReconMR Texas Poll (Sept. 17) — Talarico 49%, Paxton 43%.

Emerson College (Sept. 17) — Talarico 47%, Paxton 46%.

Mason-Dixon Polling & Research (Sept. 15) — Talarico 46%, Paxton 43%.

SoCal Strategies (Sept. 13) — Talarico 50%, Paxton 45%.

AARP (Sept. 10) — Talarico 48%, Paxton 44%.

N+ Univision (Sept. 9) — Talarico 48%, Paxton 43%.

articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: House Republicans' investigation into Democrats' main fundraising platform is heating up on the heels of an explosive report that raised questions about whether left-wing candidates' campaigns were raking in foreign cash. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed and the Democratic leaders of the House and Senate, among others. Republican lawmakers have long accused the company of having lax verification standards for donors, something ActBlue has said it actively improved since the start of the GOP's probe. But a new report released earlier this month, first reported by Fox News Digital, appears to show employees green-lighting donations despite some questions about where they came from. FAR-LEFT POLITICIANS STILL USING ACTBLUE AS 88-YEAR-OLD DISPUTES DONATING NEARLY $150,000 TO FUNDRAISING GIANT Chief among the GOP's concerns is ActBlue's passport number verification. According to the report, the field only requires the correct number of characters for a U.S. passport number rather than a valid code for a donation to be accepted. The Monday letter also points to a 2024 "contemporaneous review by ActBlue’s then-outside counsel, former Biden White House Counsel Dana Remus" which allegedly found "'a substantial risk that some of the funds' raised for Democrat campaigns and causes by ActBlue 'were impermissible contributions from foreign nationals.'" Remus' review further found that "passport checks did not always happen" and were "never conducted" when donations were made using third-party fiscal platforms like Apple Pay or PayPal, the letter said. The Republican chairs said Machen's prior comments to Congress "conceded that your 'forensic' review found that ActBlue processed and accepted donations with foreign indicators even though ActBlue failed to identify a 'passport number' or 'other indicia of eligibility' for the donor. HOUSE DEM LASHES OUT AT GOP EFFORTS TO PROBE FOREIGN DONATIONS WITH STUNNING CLAIM ON MOTIVE "Nonetheless, you defended Ms. Wallace-Jones’s representations to Congress by arguing that ActBlue’s compliance and vetting policy was 'as close to 100 percent as it could be,'" the letter said. "Documents produced to the Committees undercut your assertion. These documents demonstrate that if a donor did not have a U.S. passport or a U.S. address, an ActBlue employee retained the ability to determine an 'alternative method of verifying the [donor’s] citizenship.' This means an ActBlue employee could put 'a placeholder,' including 'ACTBLUEXX,' 'in the passport number field of [the donor’s] ActBlue account.' The placeholder allows ActBlue to accept all subsequent contributions from the donor without requiring a U.S. passport number." ACTBLUE SCRUTINY FUELS NEW GOP BILLS TO TIGHTEN ELECTION DONATION RULES The letter said Machen's review was also limited to 2023, arguing it left out potentially valuable information about 2024. "As such, the review did not accurately represent the totality of ActBlue’s foreign donation vetting and donor outreach practices during the 2024 election cycle. In fact, documents produced to the Committees show that ActBlue relaxed its vetting practices twice in 2024—data that your narrow 'forensic' review did not capture," the letter said. ACTBLUE SUES TEXAS AG KEN PAXTON, ALLEGING POLITICAL RETALIATION OVER DEMOCRATS' FUNDRAISING It also charged that he disputed Remus' analysis without going into detail on how he established his own findings. ActBlue has consistently denied any wrongdoing and dismissed Republicans' most recent findings in a statement to Fox News Digital. After we released findings of a third-party forensic analysis that completely undermined a central claim that they have made against ActBlue, Republicans are refusing to move on," ActBlue said. "Instead, they are orchestrating another political stunt before rushing out of town weeks early to go campaign. This coordinated campaign against ActBlue isn’t about the facts, or legislating, it’s about Republicans’ efforts to silence organizations they believe threaten their agenda." A closed-door interview summons is not the same as a subpoena, which is a legally binding order.

articles.title: Andrew Bailey, who joined FBI in unusual ‘co-deputy’ position, to leave bureau
articles.summary: FBI co-Deputy Director Andrew Bailey, who joined the FBI in the newly created position in September 2025 to work alongside then-Deputy Director Dan Bongino, is stepping down, two people familiar with the matter told NBC News.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — Another top FBI official is leaving the bureau after just a year on the job. Andrew Bailey, who joined the FBI in the newly created position of “co-deputy director” in September 2025 to work alongside then-Deputy Director Dan Bongino, is stepping aside, two people familiar with the matter told NBC News. Bailey confirmed his move later Monday morning on social media. An internal FBI email said Bailey was leaving for family reasons, the two people familiar with the matter said. Bailey had been the attorney general of Missouri before resigning his position to join the FBI last year. The FBI referred a request for comment to a post Bailey made on social media, stating that he wanted to thank President Donald Trump, Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel for the opportunity. “Under President Trump’s leadership, we have delivered historic results in our mission to Make America Safe Again. With great pride in what we have accomplished, I am announcing that I am stepping down to return to my family in Missouri,” Bailey wrote. “I am confident Director Patel will continue to reform the FBI, combat violent crime, defend the homeland, ensure strong organizational accountability, and restore public trust in this institution of excellence.” Bongino, a conservative podcaster and former Secret Service member, subsequently left his job to return to podcasting after just under a year at the FBI. The nontraditional co-deputy structure, set up when Bongino was in the position, remained in place. Bongino was then replaced by Chris Raia, whose background as a career FBI special agent was more in line with the tradition of having the critical No. 2 position filled by someone with extensive knowledge of the bureau. MS NOW first reported Bailey’s planned departure. Patel, who is suing The Atlantic for $250 million over an article about his leadership at the bureau, has recently gotten into heated exchanges with Democratic members of Congress over his leadership at the FBI.

articles.title: Trump administration asks Supreme Court to OK transgender inmate policy
articles.summary: The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Monday to lift a judge’s block on its policy restricting transgender inmates’ access to hormone treatments and gender-affirming surgeries. Under the Bureau of Prisons (BOP) policy, inmates currently receiving hormone treatments would be put on a tapering plan. Officials would also be required to stop providing social…
articles.body:
The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Monday to lift a judge’s block on its policy restricting transgender inmates’ access to hormone treatments and gender-affirming surgeries.

Under the Bureau of Prisons (BOP) policy, inmates currently receiving hormone treatments would be put on a tapering plan. Officials would also be required to stop providing social accommodations, like hair-removal devices, to help inmates transition.

The U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit, in a 2-1 vote , declined to lift the judge’s block, which found the policy likely illegal.

“In nullifying BOP’s exercise of its statutorily conferred authority to adopt a policy that prison administrators have determined is necessary to maintain institutional security, the court’s order causes irreparable harm to the government and to the public,” Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote in court filings.

The case heads to Supreme Court Chief Justice John Roberts, who by default manages emergency matters arising from the nation’s capital. He could act alone or refer the request to the full court for a vote.

It’s the Trump administration’s latest plea for the Supreme Court to intervene on its emergency docket to restore an aspect of the president’s agenda that a federal judge has blocked. It’s the 41st time the administration has done so since taking office, according to The Hill’s analysis of the court’s docket.

The Supreme Court has regularly ruled for Trump in emergency cases, though it hasn’t been a clean sweep. The president expressed deep frustration with some of his own appointees after the court recently refused to put Trump’s mail-in ballot plan into effect for November’s elections.

In recent years, cases implicating transgender rights have regularly reached the justices’ docket. The conservative-majority court has recently handed down major decisions enabling states to bar transgender girls from competing on women’s sports teams in schools and to restrict transgender minors from accessing gender-affirming care.

Sauer pointed to those opinions as the administration took the latest case to the high court on Monday.

“Indeed, this Court has emphasized the importance of allowing politically accountable officials to make decisions about the permissible forms of treatment for gender dysphoria,” Sauer emphasized in the government’s application.

The underlying lawsuit began last year, when transgender inmates filed a class-action challenge to officials ending their access to gender-affirming care in prison. At the current stage, the legal battle concerns a February 2026 statement the BOP issued formalizing the policy.

The directive came after Trump on his first day back in office ordered that no federal funds be spent on medical procedures “for the purpose of conforming an inmate’s appearance to that of the opposite sex.” It was part of a broader push against what his administration calls “gender ideology.”

The president’s efforts have sparked various lawsuits across the country. Last year, the Supreme Court issued an emergency order allowing the administration to enforce its ban on openly transgender troops serving in the military.

In the legal battle over transgender inmates, U.S. District Judge Royce Lamberth, an appointee of former President Reagan, has repeatedly ruled against Trump.

The administration filed its latest appeal after the D.C. Circuit voted 2-1 to uphold Lamberth’s block, agreeing that BOP’s position is likely illegal because it didn’t adequately consider its own experiences operating under its prior policy.

“For example, BOP makes claims about the security impact of providing gender-affirming care without addressing whether such issues have occurred,” the court wrote in its Sept. 18 decision.

The Trump administration rejected that in its Supreme Court appeal, calling the two-page ruling a “a perfunctory determination.” It argues BOP’s policy is legal and that the case isn’t following the procedural limits that federal law places on civil lawsuits brought by inmates.

“Tellingly, while the court of appeals asserted otherwise, it provided no explanation to support that assertion,” Sauer wrote.

articles.title: GoFundMe: ‘Factual misrepresentations’ led to end of fundraiser for man paying wife’s cancer bills
articles.summary: GoFundMe says it was her identity, not her parents’ story, that led to the fundraiser being pulled.
articles.body:
Editor’s Note: This story has been updated to correct the name of Donald Johnson .

( NewsNation ) — A GoFundMe raising money for an 81-year-old man’s wife’s cancer treatment was taken down after GoFundMe learned the “neighbor” running the campaign was actually his daughter.

She said she posed as an outsider because she thought her parents’ story would resonate more if it came from someone outside the family.

The fundraiser for Donald Johnson was deactivated after the platform said it uncovered “factual misrepresentations.” Before it was taken down, the fundraiser had raised nearly $745,000.

What led to $745K cancer fundraiser coming down?

GoFundMe told NewsNation it received a tip Sept. 25 questioning the identity of the woman running the campaign, who had identified herself only as a neighbor named “Erin.” The company’s Trust & Safety team opened an investigation, standard practice for a tip like that.

On a recorded call, GoFundMe asked the organizer directly whether Donald and Josephine were her parents. She said they were.

“Our Trust & Safety team identified factual misrepresentations, which directly violate our Terms of Service,” a GoFundMe spokesperson said in a statement.

Cancer GoFundMe shut down: Why did daughter create persona?

The organizer told GoFundMe she created the “Erin” persona because she believed her parents’ story would connect with more people if it appeared to come from a stranger moved by their situation than their own daughter asking for help. She said she filmed the video by herself and maintained that every other detail — her father’s job, her mother’s diagnosis, the financial strain — was true.

GoFundMe said misrepresenting an organizer’s identity or relationship to the beneficiary violates the platform’s terms of service, regardless of intent, because it undermines donors’ ability to know who they are giving to.

“As a result, the fundraiser has been removed and all donors have been refunded. Ensuring GoFundMe is a safe and trusted place to give and receive help is our top priority. Taking action like this allows GoFundMe to protect donors’ generosity and our continued ability to support people who are fundraising to help others,” the statement said.

Who is the couple at the center of the GoFundMe?

Johnson, 81, began working as an airport luggage courier three years ago, putting more than 200,000 miles on his car to help pay for his wife Josephine’s pancreatic cancer treatment.

“I interviewed several places, and the one that offered to hire me was this luggage carrier,” Johnson told NewsNation’s Chris Cuomo Friday.

NewsNation’s Patrick Djordevic contributed to this report.

articles.title: GOP chair of Georgia Peanut Commission backs Ossoff for Senate
articles.summary: The Republican chair of the Georgia Peanut Commission is backing Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff (Ga.) in his bid for a second full term. “We don’t necessarily elect a party,” commission Chair Donald Chase told The Atlanta Journal-Constitution. “I like to support people that I can get behind and believe in.” Chase, whom board members elected…
articles.body:
The Republican chair of the Georgia Peanut Commission is backing Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff (Ga.) in his bid for a second full term.

“We don’t necessarily elect a party,” commission Chair Donald Chase told The Atlanta Journal-Constitution . “I like to support people that I can get behind and believe in.”

Chase, whom board members elected as chair of the Georgia Peanut Commission in January, is a lifelong Republican who is still supporting and contributing to other GOP candidates in the November midterms, the Journal-Constitution reported.

The Georgia Peanut Commission, led by five elected board members, conducts promotional, research and educational programs regarding the Peach State’s peanut industry. Last year, Georgia farmers produced more than half of the peanuts in the U.S., according to the commission .

Ossoff, the youngest senator, is seeking reelection against two-term Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.). Most polling has the incumbent comfortably in the lead, while The Hill’s data partner, Decision Desk HQ , gives Ossoff an 86 percent chance to win.

While President Trump backed Collins in his June primary runoff against former football coach Derek Dooley, multiple local Republicans have thrown their support behind Ossoff.

Julie Smith and Scott James Matheson — the GOP mayors of Tifton, Ga., and Valdosta, Ga., respectively — have endorsed the Democratic senator, who is a frequent critic of the president and who sits on the Senate Appropriations and Intelligence committees.

Former GOP Sen. Jeff Flake (Ariz.), an anti-Trump Republican and former U.S. ambassador to Turkey, also endorsed Ossoff last month.

“I’m still a conservative Republican. But character matters. And I want someone in that seat who takes the institution seriously and will protect the institution,” Flake told the Journal-Constitution .

Ossoff has repeatedly said he is not considering a 2028 presidential run , telling MS NOW’s Jen Psaki last month he has “zero interest” in seeking the Democratic nomination.

The first Democratic primary in South Carolina is set for roughly a year after Ossoff would begin a second term, if he defeats Collins in November.

articles.title: What will winter be like near you? Here’s what the outlooks suggest
articles.summary: Will you need a parka and a shovel or an umbrella and a sweater this winter?
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – In life, there are few certain things, but we can guarantee at least one certainty: winter is coming.

Sure, the calendar shows it’s only the end of September. The leaves may only just be changing near you, and temperatures may still be tolerable without a jacket. But we’ve never been closer to the 2026-2027 winter season than we are now.

So what will it look like near you? That isn’t exactly a guarantee.

You could be buried in snow, battling frigid temperatures. Or maybe it will be a dry year with temperatures that don’t fall to total bitterness. It depends on who you ask.

The Old Farmer’s Almanac and Farmers’ Almanac have again released their extended forecasts for the impending winter season. The latter calls for “snow, sleet and surprises,” while the former suggests we will experience a mild winter with “colder, snowier spots.”

More specifically, the Farmers’ Almanac reports that its formula is predicting winter precipitation throughout the seven main regions of the U.S. In the upper Plains and Midwest, that’s “snowy” precipitation. It will be “wet” across the Gulf and southern East Coast and “wetter” in the South with “coastal storms” in New England.

Meanwhile, the Old Farmer’s Almanac’s outlook emphasizes mildness for most of the U.S. Only the Ohio Valley region and southern New England are forecast to have a “cold winter,” per the periodical’s formula, while Hawaii could be “cool.”

Most of the Plains will remain dry as the Pacific Coast, parts of the Gulf, and the Midwest are expected to be wet, according to the outlook.

Whether or not you believe these forecasts, research has shown only about half of the forecasts produced by the Farmers’ Almanac were correct. Both publications claim to be 80% accurate with their long-range forecasts.

“It’s more like a crapshoot of trusting something that far into the future since there are times the forecast is blown in the first 24 hours,” meteorologist Rich Segal, who recently retired from Nexstar’s KXAN, previously explained.

What about the National Weather Service?

The National Weather Service also offers long-range weather outlooks, but even those are subject to change. They also don’t predict specific events, like major winter storms.

“It’s just not possible to do that,” Jon Gottschalck, Operational Prediction Branch Chief at NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center, told Nexstar.

The Climate Prediction Center earlier this month released updated seasonal forecasts outlining what kind of broad weather patterns we can expect through the end of 2026 . For most of us, the outlook suggests we’re likely to see warmer-than-normal temperatures (unsurprisingly, thanks to the supercharged El Niño that could be sticking around ). A large band of states, primarily in the South, are leaning toward above-average precipitation from October through December.

The outlook for November, December, and January is about the same. A large swath of the U.S. is likely to see warmer-than-normal temperatures into the start of 2027, while an expansive band of states is leaning toward above-average precipitation. You can view the seasonal temperature and precipitation outlooks for November through January in the slideshow below:

NOAA, the Farmer’s Almanac and the Old Farmer’s Almanac do review some of the same factors. That includes what could become the strongest El Niño pattern we’ve seen since 1950 . The phenomenon is nearly certain to last into spring 2027 , according to the latest climate models.

As we head into winter, how El Niño plays out will be very different for the northern half of the country and the southern half . Broadly speaking, the northern states will be drier and warmer than normal, while southern states will be cooler and wetter.

“We can still get occasional shots of colder air that drop into the central U.S., and we’re still going to get cold air to go across the northern Plains, and yes, there’s still going to be at least some snow across the northern part of the U.S., but the overall pattern does not favor a whole lot of snow across the northern U.S.,” Brian James, Nexstar chief meteorologist, said last week.

So can you trust the almanac predictions? Ultimately, it’s up to you.

“While no forecast can claim perfect accuracy, our predictions have proven useful for generations of planners and outdoor enthusiasts,” Sandi Duncan, the editor of the Farmers’ Almanac, told Nexstar last year. “We continuously refine our method but acknowledge that Mother Nature always has the final say.”

Nexstar’s Alix Martichoux contributed to this report.

articles.title: The West must win its future wars and not just battles
articles.summary: Let us verify that China and Russia are indeed the threats we believe they are before taking any future action we may regret.
articles.body:
Last week, the London Defense Conference came to Washington for a second year. Founded in 2022 in response to Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, the event “is committed to strengthening defense in the light of evolving threats from authoritarian regimes.”

This year’s topic was winning future wars, and the unanswered questions remain. Can the West and the U.S. prevail in current and future conflicts? The record beyond winning the Cold War — if it was really won, or if the Soviet Union imploded under the reform efforts imposed by Mikhail Gorbachev — is unimpressive .

The war in Iran is proving disastrous for the United States. Despite extraordinary heroism and endurance, can 29 million Ukrainians stave off the assaults of Russia, which has a population of over 140 million and has so far sustained 1.5 million killed and wounded?

The West’s only real victory was Britain’s defeat of Argentina in the 1982 Falklands War . Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher ordered Operation Corporate to sail 6,000 miles to reoccupy a relatively small collection of islands in the South Atlantic that had been seized by Argentina.

Of course, the world has changed. Warfare has been transformed, and the battlefield has been equalized by drones, missiles and artificial intelligence. Militarily weak states and groups now possess formidable capabilities that, so far, can only be countered by very expensive weapons. For example, a relatively cheap ballistic missile can be destroyed by the U.S. Navy’s SM-3 missile . But that missile costs over $27 million.

To deal with battlefields irrespective of locale, cheaper weapons and uncrewed systems have assumed a high priority. In the spirit of the old saying, never send a man where you can send a bullet; unmanned surface, sub-surface and aviation units will save lives.

But what happens when uncrewed weapons systems approach the costs of manned systems? And while unmanned drones can save lives, these systems are also Ukraine’s most dangerous battlefield killers.

The conference began a dialogue that the U.S. must consider. I have written before about why the U.S. has lost every war it started since the end of World War II. No matter the political party in charge, the causes were the same.

While each party was a contributor, defeat arose from a lack of knowledge and understanding about how military force can achieve a strategic outcome. Hubris in the belief that American military superiority would prevail, transposing our views on what we believed an enemy would do instead of what they actually did, political expediency and crippling bureaucracy all contributed.

From Vietnam, where Lyndon Johnson said the U.S. fought an imminent threat from communism, to Iraq, where Saddam Hussein did not have weapons of mass destruction, the reasons for going to war proved dead wrong.

In Afghanistan, hunting Osama bin Laden became nation building — a mission impossible. And in attacking Iran, the administration did not anticipate the near-certain threat of Iran closing the Strait of Hormuz, or Tehran attacking U.S. allies in the Gulf and expanding the war to Yemen .

Both Republican and Democratic administrations were guilty of errors. How can we reduce the chances that future administrations do not repeat these blunders? Currently, China is the main U.S. adversary. America’s aim is to defend Taiwan from an invasion despite its policy of strategic ambiguity.

Europe is fearful that after Ukraine, Vladimir Putin may attack west, seizing one of the Baltic states or a nearby island, even Svalbard off Norway’s coast. But are these fears exaggerated, like the threat of a monolithic Communist threat in the 1960s, Iraqi weapons of mass destruction and possibly Iran’s pursuit of nuclear weapons? While we may never have absolute answers, analyzing the possibilities is essential.

As Ronald Reagan said , “trust, but verify.” Let us verify that China and Russia are indeed the threats we believe they are before taking any future action we may regret.

Harlan Ullman is chairman of a private company and principal author of the doctrine of shock and awe. His next book, co-written with Field Marshal The Lord David Richards, former United Kingdom chief of defense, is “Who Thinks Best Wins: How Decisive Strategic Thinking Will Prevent Global Chaos. “

articles.title: Trump unveils plans for a $15 billion steel mill in Iowa
articles.summary: President Donald Trump on Monday announced a plan for a $15 billion steel mill in Iowa.
articles.body: President Donald Trump on Monday announced a plan for a $15 billion steel mill in Iowa. “This steel will be mined, melted, and made right here in the USA, which is something very unusual,” Trump said in the Oval Office, where he was joined by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick; Joe Broking, the CEO of the company building the plant; and other business leaders. Mesabi Metallics is constructing the plant with the aim of starting production by 2030, a White House official said. The facility is expected to produce 10 million tons of steel a year and create as many as 1,750 permanent jobs in the state, the official said. The plant will be capable of supporting defense sector requirements for high-grade steel, the official said. The president claimed the plant will “produce some of the highest quality, most affordable steel anywhere in the world.” The Wall Street Journal was first to report on the new facility. The plant will use iron ore from a new mine that the company invested $2.5 billion to build in Minnesota. The mine, which will come on line in the coming weeks, will produce about 7.5 million tons of iron per year and create about 350 jobs in the state, the White House official said. The mine is based in Minnesota’s Mesabi Iron Range, which stretches 80 to 100 miles and contributed about 60% of total iron ore production in the U.S. during the 20th century, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. “It’s the first new iron ore mine in the United States in more than 50 years,” Trump said. The Export-Import Bank, the federal government’s export credit agency, will issue up to $10 billion in financing for Mesabi Metallics’ expansion there, an agency release said. Trump has prioritized the expansion of the U.S. manufacturing sector, including by taking aim at steel imports as part of a wide-ranging trade policy. Although the Supreme Court earlier this year struck down many of the tariffs he imposed, it did leave duties in place on imported steel and aluminum. The U.S. currently levies a 50% tariff on most steel imports. Trump on Monday touted his efforts to try to reinvigorate the industry. “Soon after my inauguration, I imposed powerful 50% tariffs on all foreign steel, and now our steel industry is roaring back to life,” he said. “Everyone’s building their plant here because they don’t want to pay tariffs.” In a letter to Trump last week, steel industry groups urged the president to “stand firm against efforts to weaken the tariffs” as U.S. steelmakers invest in new mills domestically. “Weakening the tariffs now would put that progress at risk, threatening American jobs and the economic and national security benefits the policy was designed to protect,” they warned.

articles.title: Reporter's Notebook: Senate Republicans scrap early exit from Washington as midterm stakes soar
articles.summary: Senate Republicans force a test vote on the Ratepayer Protection Act, daring Democrats to block a data center affordability bill boosting Jon Husted.
articles.body: It’s a calculation by Republicans to keep the Senate in session this week. Yes. The Senate was scheduled to meet anyway over the next few days. But the general consensus early last week was that the Senate would be done then, and those facing competitive races would be back home campaigning. Then Wednesday hit. Republicans wanted to stay in Washington. For a very specific reason. And many of them told Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., as much at their weekly luncheon. "Odds are we plan on being here next week," said Thune. REPORTER'S NOTEBOOK: CONGRESS STRUGGLES TO FIND A MESSAGE THAT RESONATES WITH VOTERS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS One Senate aide compared the Senate’s schedule to a cat chasing a beam of light from a laser pointer. But the Senate is in fact meeting. There are reasons. Most of them are political. The Senate wasn’t quite done with the bill to regulate money in intercollegiate athletics last week. And with the affordability question vexing Republicans, they really didn’t want to pass the college sports bill and promptly vacate Washington. That would be an awkward punctuation point at the end of the legislative sentence before the midterms. GOPers wanted something more substantive. Democrats might have presented that opportunity to Republicans on a platter. Before the House left for the midterms the week before last, it accentuated its session by passing the Ratepayer Protection Act, 417-3. Let me tell you, not much passes around here with 417 votes. Like their Senate colleagues, House Republicans also worry about voters doubting they’re addressing affordability. So this bill hit the mark for them. The legislation defrays the costs ratepayers fork out for their utility bills if they’re driven up by data centers. This forces the tech companies which run the data centers to foot the bill. Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio, is one of the most vulnerable Republicans on the ballot this fall. Husted’s longtime support for data centers is also dragging him down in the eyes of some voters. Husted tried to fix that. He went to the floor and asked for the Senate to pass on the spot the House bill. However, Sen. Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., objected, blocking the effort. FOX NEWS POLL: ECONOMIC ANXIETY AND CANDIDATE CONCERNS DEFINE OHIO SENATE RACE Republicans viewed that as an opening. Democrats stood in the way of passing a bill on affordability which 417 bipartisan House members supported without blinking. Senate GOPers immediately seized this opportunity as a wedge against their adversaries. And, they interpreted this as a chance to assist their Ohio colleague. "Tell the data centers we're happy to have you. But you've got to pay your own electricity. People are not going to pay for it," said Sen. John Kennedy, R-La. Republicans were already leery about the uneven political footing when it comes to AI. Even more so with data centers. Voters are not enamored with the results of the Big, Beautiful Bill, passed last summer. But dealing with data centers is more immediate and might resonate with those who soured on the Republican brand. "In Missouri, people are absolutely scared to death that these data centers are going to take all the prime farm ground of the state. And then they're going to raise electricity bills so high, no one will be able to afford them," said Sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo. The official schedule intended for the Senate to meet this week. But once September hit and no government shutdown loomed, senators from both sides – especially those facing challenging elections – wanted to skip Washington and campaign back home. Yours truly asked Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., why his party stood in the way of the Senate aligning with the House on that data center/utilities measure. "Was this blocked in the Senate last week by Democrats as an effort to prevent Sen. Husted from having a win in this competitive race?" I asked. "Sen. Husted's bill is a fraud. It's voluntary. No company has to do it. The bill we have is mandatory. It is much stronger and is what is needed," replied Schumer. There is something to Schumer’s argument about how muscular the bill is. The legislation says public utility regulators must only consider a standard for ratepayers. Nothing is required. Thus, there’s wiggle room for tech firms. HAWLEY TAKES AIM AT 'CORPORATE WELFARE' AFTER GOP-BACKED TAX BREAK BOOSTED CONTROVERSIAL INDUSTRY "What we're saying is that we can do much better," said Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md. "Is it a little step forward? Yes. But it's not meeting the moment. So our view is we should expand it to make sure that ratepayers aren't having to subsidize the richest corporations on the planet." But a lot of Republicans aren’t buying what Schumer and Van Hollen are saying. The Democratic objections are all about three things: Politics. An endangered GOP senator in the most expensive Senate contest in the country. And, Democrats are hoping to flip the seat in their favor. "Sen. Schumer, what he cares about is the midterm election and politics. And I don't think he cares about the substance of this," said Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas. "Obviously there's a hot and heavy Senate race going on in Ohio, and he doesn't want to let Sen. Husted have something he can talk about when he goes home." Republicans view the opportunity to turn the affordability issue against Democrats – capitalizing on Schumer’s remark and forcing Democrats to take a stand. Either you’re for affordability (especially as it pertains to the toxic issue of data centers) or you’re not. Moreover, this could boost Husted in his competitive contest with former Sen. Sherrod Brown, D-Ohio. In fact, it was the Senate GOP’s campaign arm which specifically flagged vulnerabilities for Republicans generally and Husted in particular over the summer. Thune tees up a test vote on Wednesday to dare Democrats to either start debate on the bill or block it again. That vote requires 60 yeas. So Democratic cooperation is required. Although there’s skepticism anything happens, some Democrats may vote for it. That means the Senate is on the bill. And it’s open to debate and amendments. Thune would have to forge a bipartisan time agreement to finish the measure quickly. Otherwise – by the book – this would drag into the weekend. And no one wants that. Especially Republicans with competitive races. 12 RACES SCRAMBLE SENATE BATTLEFIELD AS DEMOCRATS EYE COMEBACK Thune and Schumer want senators back home campaigning. If Democrats impede the legislation Wednesday, the Senate might hang around Thursday or that’s it until after the midterms. Regardless, Republicans will have engineered a vote which they can boomerang against Democrats. Or, at least help Husted and send him back to the Buckeye State with a win. While it’s not the best optic for Democrats to oppose this bill, their resistance might not directly wound anyone this fall. The reason: Democrats have a lot of chances to pick up seats. articles.title: In reversal, Justice Samuel Alito steps aside from major climate case
articles.summary: Conservative Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito will no longer participate in a major climate case after facing calls because of his stock holdings in oil companies.
articles.body: WASHINGTON — Conservative Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito will no longer participate in a major climate change case after facing calls that he recuse himself because of his stock holdings in oil companies. The new development was disclosed in a letter dated Monday and sent to lawyers involved in the case, with no reason given. “Justice Alito has determined that he will not continue to participate in this case,” the letter said. Alito had, via a court spokeswoman, previously told NBC News there was no need for him to step aside from the case, which is being argued next week and could have broad nationwide implications when the court issues a ruling. Left-leaning groups have repeatedly called for Alito’s recusal from the case, in which ExxonMobil and Suncor Energy are seeking to toss out a Colorado lawsuit seeking damages from the oil companies for the impacts of climate change. Although Alito does not own stocks in either company, he does hold stocks in oil companies ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66, as well as five other firms involved in the energy sector, his financial disclosure report says. Activists calling for his recusal said the companies he holds stocks in could benefit if the Supreme Court throws out the Colorado case, brought by the city and county of Boulder, because it could directly affect similar cases across the country in which they are among the defendants. The court has a 6-3 conservative majority. With Alito stepping aside, it raises the possibility of a 4-4 split, which would leave the major legal issues unresolved. The oil and gas industry is hoping the court will issue a broad ruling that would prevent cases like the one in Colorado from moving forward in state courts, potentially saving it from paying out billions of dollars in damages. Earlier in the litigation, in 2023, Alito did recuse himself when the court turned away an appeal from the companies in the Colorado case. On the same day, the court rejected appeals in similar cases involving other companies, including ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66. Alito also did not participate in those cases. In May, a court spokesman said Alito had “inadvertently recused” in the earlier Colorado case. “Justice Alito does not have a financial interest in any party” involved in the case, the court spokeswoman said in a statement provided to NBC News at the time. Alito was advised by the court’s legal counsel that “his recusal is not required,” she added. That was before the most recent calls for Alito to step aside based on the indirect benefit he could obtain from a ruling in favor of Exxon and Suncor. Earlier this month, an advocacy group called Consumer Watchdog pointed to disclosures made by ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66 to shareholders in which they warned of the risks the companies face as a result of climate lawsuits making similar claims to the Colorado case. “Justice Alito’s recusal ... is the right decision, and one he should have made from the start,” Alexandra Nagy, the group’s organizing director, said in a statement. The Supreme Court spokeswoman did not immediately respond to a request seeking further comment. Some conservatives have also pushed for liberal Justice Elena Kagan to recuse herself in the case because of a controversy over a chapter on climate change included in, and subsequently removed from, a reference manual for judges. Kagan wrote a brief foreword to the manual and recently told lawmakers that she never read the chapter in question.

articles.title: US Supreme Court's Alito won't participate in climate case involving oil companies
articles.summary: By John Kruzel WASHINGTON, Sept 28 (Reuters) - US Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito will not participate in an upcoming case involving a bid by oil companie...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON, Sept 28 (Reuters) - US Supreme Court Justice Samuel Alito will not participate in an upcoming case involving a bid ‌by oil companies to scuttle a lawsuit seeking to hold them liable ‌for helping fuel climate change, a court official said on Monday.

Alito owns stock in several ​oil and gas companies but not Exxon Mobil and Suncor Energy, the two companies involved in the dispute to be heard by the court on October 5. He had initially declined calls from watchdog and environmental groups to recuse. Alito stepped ‌aside when the litigation reached ⁠the court at an earlier stage in 2023.

Alito is one of the most conservative justices on the court, which has ⁠a 6-3 conservative majority.

Lawyers for the oil companies and those representing officials in Boulder, Colorado, who sued Exxon and Suncor in 2018, were informed on Monday of ​Alito's recusal ​in a letter from Scott Harris, clerk ​of the Supreme Court.

Harris did ‌not provide a rationale, stating only, "I am writing to inform the parties that Justice Alito has determined that he will not continue to participate in this case."

The dispute, which will be heard on the first day of the court's new term, could determine the fate of dozens of state and local climate-related ‌lawsuits against fossil fuel companies.

According to his most ​recent financial disclosure, Alito's holdings include stock in ​ConocoPhillips and Phillips 66, which are ​defendants in separate but similar climate-related lawsuits.

The upcoming Supreme Court ‌case involves whether federal law precludes ​certain claims under ​state law seeking damages for harms allegedly caused by the effects of greenhouse gas emissions. The justices also directed the parties to address whether ​the court has jurisdiction ‌to decide the case at this stage.

President Donald Trump's administration has ​backed Exxon and Suncor, arguing that federal law precludes Boulder's claims.

(Reporting ​by John Kruzel; Editing by Will Dunham)

articles.body: Vice President JD Vance wants to drastically change the H-1B foreign worker visa program in favor of a system that prioritizes American workers rather than the one he says currently displaces members of the domestic workforce. "So, what are the things we can do administratively to ensure that if a tech company is going to try to get an H-1B visa, it's an actual genius, it's a person that is going to significantly enrich the tech ecosystem or the American economy?" AMERICA’S BROKEN LEGAL IMMIGRATION SYSTEM IS REPLACING US WORKERS BY DESIGN H-1B visas are temporary nonimmigrant programs that allow foreign workers in "specialty occupations," often referred to as "high-skilled workers," to come to the United States and work, typically for three years, according to United States Customs and Immigration Services (USCIS). But critics say the program has been abused by large companies, many in the tech industry, to simply replace Americans in the workforce with cheaper labor from abroad. Many also argue that the visa recipients aren't better suited than American workers to do the jobs. Vance said the administration is trying to ensure companies are, "not just replacing one accountant who makes $60,000 with a lower-wage foreign accountant who makes $45,000 a year." CEO UNDER FIRE FOR MASS LAYOFFS AMID FOREIGN WORKER HIRING SPREE NOW APPOINTED TO FED'S TASK FORCE ON JOBS "We're also looking at various ways of preventing companies that use H-1B visas from laying off a bunch of American workers," said Vance in a clip shared on Sunday that sparked chatter on social media. "So, one of the things that I find just shocking about this is that you'll have a company that applies for an H-1B, and they'll say, 'oh, we're desperate for workers, we can't find the workers,' and then you go and look at their history and they've laid off 5,000 people," he explained. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) announced in August a new rule to charge $103,265 to companies as an additional fee for every H-1B petition subject to the annual statutory cap of 65,000 per year. FEDERAL JUDGE STRIKES DOWN TRUMP’S $100K H-1B VISA FEE, RULING IT AN UNCONSTITUTIONAL TAX A similar proposal from the administration was previously struck down by a federal district court. "So, we're doing a lot, within the confines of course of what we're allowed to do legally. We've gotten sued on some of this stuff. But I think fundamentally, we're on [sic] the right on both the law and the policy."
